mind if.meaning: A polite way to ask for permission; 'do you object if'.
mind if.example: Mind if I take a look around?

be my guest.meaning: Said to tell someone they are welcome to do something; 'go ahead'.

train on.meaning: To point or aim something, like a camera, at a person or thing.
train on.example: He trains his camera on the gleaming blade.

go to one's head.meaning: If praise goes to your head, it makes you too proud.
go to one's head.example: Bob says don’t let it go to my head.

put under.meaning: To make a person or animal unconscious with drugs, usually for an operation.
put under.example: “We’re going to need to put this one under,” he says.

quick study.meaning: A person who learns new things fast.

have an opening.meaning: To have a job that no one is doing yet; a job vacancy.
have an opening.example: But the zoo lady said maybe they’ll have an opening there in a while, cleaning cages and stuff.

bathed in.meaning: Covered by something soft like light or color.
bathed in.example: There I am: the One and Only Ivan, bathed in the pink light of dawn.

thanks for nothing.meaning: Said angrily to mean the opposite of thanks; 'you helped with nothing'.
thanks for nothing.example: He says thanks for nothing, George.

by the way.example: Ivan and Kinyani are real gorillas—and so, by the way, is Jambo, whose story Stella tells to Ivan and Bob.
by the way.meaning: Incidentally; said when adding a small extra thought.

clear one's throat.meaning: To cough a little, often before speaking or when nervous.

come to.meaning: To wake up; to become conscious again after sleep or a drug.

from time to time.example: They are a contented group, placid and good-natured, although, like any family, they bicker from time to time.
from time to time.meaning: Sometimes; now and then, but not often.

get the hang of.example: I’m not sure I will ever get the hang of it.
get the hang of.meaning: To learn how to do something; to become able to do it well.

get this.example: And get this: they’re all poodles.

in the flesh.meaning: In person; really here, not in a picture or a dream.

just in case.example: He licks my chin, just in case there are any leftovers.
just in case.meaning: To be ready for something that might happen.

make a move.meaning: To do something to start a romance; to flirt.

might as well.example: Might as well stay one more night.
might as well.meaning: It is sensible to do something; there is no good reason not to.

most of all.example: But most of all, I miss Bob.

one's stomach drops.meaning: To suddenly feel scared or sick with worry.

one's turn.meaning: The time when it is your turn to do something, in order.

out of the corner of one's eye.example: Out of the corner of my eye, I see someone running.
out of the corner of one's eye.meaning: At the edge of what you can see, without looking straight at it.

pop out.example: A tiny, nut-brown, big-eared head pops out of Julia’s backpack.
pop out.meaning: To appear suddenly from inside something.

take in.example: I take in the wall, splattered and splashed with mud.
take in.meaning: To look at something carefully and notice it fully.

take shape.example: When I started to write about the grim facts of Ivan’s solitary existence, a new tale slowly began to take shape.
take shape.meaning: To develop and become clear; to start having a real form.

me ball.meaning: a ball made of dried animal waste that Ivan throws at visitors
me ball.here: Ivan throws a me-ball at the visitors watching him.
me ball.example: A me-ball is made by rolling up dung until it’s the size of a small apple, then letting it dry.

paragraphs.context: The names are mine, but they’re not me.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan's nicknames are his, but they are not who he really is. He is just Ivan.
paragraphs.simple: People have given Ivan many names. The names belong to him, but they are not him. He is Ivan — just Ivan, only Ivan.

paragraphs.context: but understanding human speech is not the same as understanding humans
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan understands human words, but understanding words is not the same as understanding humans.
paragraphs.simple: Over the years, Ivan has learned what human words mean. But to understand the sounds people make is not the same as to understand the people themselves.

paragraphs.context: They hear fighting words on the wind, when all I’m thinking is
paragraphs.mainIdea: People see Ivan's size as a challenge, but he is only thinking about the beauty of the late-day sun.
paragraphs.simple: When humans look at how big Ivan is, they feel tested, as if he wants to fight. They imagine angry words in the air. But Ivan is not thinking about fighting at all. He is only thinking about how the low sun reminds him of a ripe, sweet fruit.

paragraphs.context: in a human habitat called the Exit 8 Big Top Mall and Video Arcade
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan lives in a shopping mall with a circus, next to the highway. The show runs three times a day, every day of the year.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan's home is a human place called the Exit 8 Big Top Mall and Video Arcade. It is easy to reach, just off the highway called I-95. The circus show happens at two, four, and seven o'clock, every one of the 365 days of the year.

paragraphs.context: I live here because I am too much gorilla and not enough human.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan's "domain" is his cage at one end of the circus ring. He lives there because a gorilla does not fit into the human world.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan calls his cage his domain — his own space. It stands at one end of the circus ring. He lives there because he is too much of a gorilla and not enough of a human to live anywhere else.

paragraphs.context: beckons them to stop and rest like gazelles at a watering hole
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan imagines the endless cars on the highway as a wild herd, and the mall's big sign as something calling them to rest.
paragraphs.simple: Past the parking lot there is a highway full of cars that keep coming without end. Ivan pictures them like wild animals running together. At the edge of the road stands a giant sign. It seems to call out to the cars, asking them to stop and rest — the way a pool of water in the wild calls to thirsty gazelles.

paragraphs.context: When my father beat his chest, it was to say
paragraphs.mainIdea: A silverback uses anger to keep order and protect his family. Ivan's father beat his chest to show he was in charge.
paragraphs.simple: Anger is a valuable tool for a silverback, the head of a gorilla family. He uses it to keep order and to warn his family of danger. When Ivan's father hit his chest with his hands, he was saying: watch out, listen to me, I am the boss. He showed anger to protect his family, because that is what a silverback is born to do.

paragraphs.context: Stella told me that some circuses move from town to town.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stella describes traveling circuses: performers on ropes, lions, and long lines of elephants holding tails.
paragraphs.simple: Stella says some circuses move from town to town. They have humans who hang from ropes twisting down from the tops of tents. They have lions that make angry noises and show shining teeth. And they have long lines of elephants, each one holding the limp tail of the elephant in front. The elephants stare far into the distance so they will not see the humans who want to see them.

paragraphs.context: They hunt frantically, stalking, pushing, grumbling.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan sees shoppers as hunters chasing things to buy — but however much they carry home, they always come back for more.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan watches humans rush from store to store. He describes them like hunters: moving fast, pushing each other, making angry noises. They leave holding bags full of bright things, soft things, big things. But no matter how full the bags are, they always return to get more.

paragraphs.context: The man wipes the glass and then I am gone.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Each night a man wipes Ivan's noseprint off the glass, and Ivan feels that he disappears too.
paragraphs.simple: The man wipes the glass wall clean, and then Ivan is gone. His noseprint disappears, and with it, Ivan feels that he himself disappears too — as if no one can see him.

paragraphs.context: is made by rolling up dung until it’s the size of a small apple
paragraphs.mainIdea: A me-ball is a ball of dried dung that Ivan rolls, dries, and keeps ready to throw at visitors.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan makes me-balls from dung. He rolls the dung into a ball as big as a small apple, then lets it dry. He always keeps a few of them ready to throw.

paragraphs.context: She draws the ideas in her head. I draw the things in my cage
paragraphs.mainIdea: Julia draws imaginary things from her mind, while Ivan only draws the plain objects in his cage.
paragraphs.simple: Julia draws the ideas in her head — things that are not real. Ivan cannot do that. His drawings are pale and shy next to hers. He draws only the simple things in his cage that fill his days: an apple core, a banana peel, a candy wrapper. He often eats the things he draws before he draws them.

paragraphs.context: Mack soon realized that people will pay for a picture made by a gorilla
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mack learned that people will pay for a gorilla's drawings, so now Ivan must draw every day.
paragraphs.simple: Mack found out that visitors will pay money for a picture made by a gorilla, even if they cannot tell what it shows. So now Ivan draws every day. His works sell for twenty dollars each — twenty-five with a frame — at the gift shop near his cage.

paragraphs.context: With enough time, you can get used to almost anything.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan wishes he could tell the boy that a hard life becomes bearable with time.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan wanted to tell the little boy: it is not so bad. With enough time, you can get used to almost anything — you can learn to live with a hard life.

paragraphs.context: Isn’t the way they stare at me, sitting in my tiny box
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan wonders whether humans staring at him in his cage is just as strange as a gorilla watching TV.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan wonders about something. People stare at him while he sits in his tiny box — his cage. Is that not just as strange as a gorilla staring at tiny humans in a box?

paragraphs.context: If you do not, the claw-stick comes swinging.
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the circus, Stella earned a treat for doing her trick — and was hit with a sharp claw-stick when she did not.
paragraphs.simple: Stella is talking about life as a circus elephant. If she stood on her back legs while a dog jumped on her head, she got a treat. If she did not do the trick, the trainers hit her with a claw-stick — a stick with a sharp hook that came swinging at her.

paragraphs.context: from the chains she wore as a youth: her bracelets, she calls them
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stella's legs still carry scars from the chains of her youth — scars she sadly calls her "bracelets."
paragraphs.simple: Stella's legs show old scars in circles, left by the chains she wore when she was young. She calls those scars her bracelets — a sad joke, because a bracelet is a pretty thing people choose to wear, and she never chose the chains. At the circus she had to stand on a small platform for her hardest trick. One day she fell and hurt her foot, and when she could no longer keep up, the circus sold her to Mack.

paragraphs.context: It has meanings within meanings, like human words.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bob's tail is hard to read — it can mean many feelings at once, the way human words do.
paragraphs.simple: Bob's tail makes Ivan dizzy and confused. It has meanings inside meanings, the way human words do. "I am sad," it says. "I am happy." It also says, "Watch out! I may be tiny, but my teeth are sharp."

paragraphs.context: “There’s a difference,” Stella says gently, “between ‘can’t remember’ and ‘won’t remember.’”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stella suggests that Ivan is not unable to remember his past — he is unwilling to.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan says he cannot remember much about his past. Stella answers gently: there is a difference between not being able to remember and not wanting to remember.

paragraphs.context: They help tell us who we are.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stella says memories are precious because they help tell us who we are.
paragraphs.simple: Stella tells Ivan that memories are like treasure. They help us know who we are. She asks him to try remembering his keepers — the humans who took care of him over the years. He always liked Karl, the one with the harmonica.

paragraphs.context: is a large domain. A wild cage. A safe place to be.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stella describes a good zoo as a big, safe place where animals can roam — a way for humans to make up for past wrongs.
paragraphs.simple: Stella says a good zoo is a large domain — a wild cage, a safe place to be. It has room to roam, and humans who do not hurt the animals. A good zoo, she says, is how humans make amends — how they try to make up for bad things they have done.

paragraphs.context: This gal is gonna sell us some tickets.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mack introduces the baby elephant Ruby, hoping she will sell tickets and save his failing business.
paragraphs.simple: Mack shouts for everyone to stand back: a new animal has arrived. This is Ruby, a baby elephant. Mack jokes that she is six hundred pounds of fun. He bought her because cute babies bring visitors, and visitors buy tickets. He needs the money.

paragraphs.context: “it will never, ever be okay,” and I know enough to stop talking
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stella is deeply upset about the baby elephant's arrival, and Ivan knows he should stop talking.
paragraphs.simple: Stella tells Ivan that things will never, ever be okay. Ivan understands from her tone that he should not argue or comfort her now, so he stops talking.

paragraphs.context: but I got her cheap from this bankrupt circus out west
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mack bought Ruby cheaply from a failed circus, counting on cute babies to make him rich.
paragraphs.simple: Mack says Ruby is not the finest elephant, but he got her for little money from a circus in the west that went out of business. They had brought her from Africa only a month before. Mack says people love babies — baby elephants, baby gorillas, even a baby alligator — because babies sell tickets and can make him a rich man.

paragraphs.context: “To break her spirit,” Stella says. “So she could learn to balance
paragraphs.mainIdea: Circus trainers chained baby Ruby almost all day to crush her will, so she would learn tricks.
paragraphs.simple: Stella explains why the circus chained Ruby up. They wanted to break her spirit — to crush her courage and her wish to fight back. Then she would learn to stand on a small platform, to stand on her back legs, and to let a dog jump on her back while she walked round and round without thinking.

paragraphs.context: “Before the circus, I used to live with my mom and my aunts
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ruby tells Ivan that her whole elephant family in the wild is dead.
paragraphs.simple: Ruby says that before the circus, she lived in the wild with her mother, her aunts, her sisters, and her cousins. While she talks, she picks up a piece of hay, drops it, picks it up again, and spins it. Then she says: they are dead.

paragraphs.context: “Who else?” Bob asks, and we all fall silent.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bob's bitter question means everyone knows who killed Ruby's family, and no one wants to speak.
paragraphs.simple: Bob asks, “Who else?” His question sounds bitter, as if the answer is plain to everyone. Then Ivan, Bob, and Ruby all fall silent.

paragraphs.context: When I’m drawing a picture, I feel … quiet inside.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan tells Ruby something he has never told anyone: drawing makes him feel calm and peaceful inside.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan stops for a moment. He has never talked to anyone about this before. He tells Ruby: when I am drawing a picture, I feel quiet inside myself. Making art gives him a calm, peaceful feeling.

paragraphs.context: he wasn’t really such a sound sleeper after all.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A memory comes back to Ivan, and he suddenly understands: his father was probably only pretending to be a deep sleeper.
paragraphs.simple: A memory flashes past and surprises Ivan. He remembers his father, snoring peacefully in the sun while Ivan tried every trick he knew to wake him. Now Ivan realizes something new: perhaps his father was not really such a deep sleeper. Perhaps he was only pretending, letting Ivan try to wake him as a game.

paragraphs.context: Money’s tight, though. Can’t be calling the vet every time she sneezes.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mack will not call the animal doctor, because money is short. He will not pay a vet for every small problem.
paragraphs.simple: Mack says Stella’s sore foot never heals right. He will watch it, but money is tight. He cannot call the animal doctor every time Stella sneezes — every time she has a small problem. George asked Mack to look at Stella’s foot, but Mack does not want to spend the money.

paragraphs.context: If humans are so swell, who did that to her?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bob asks a hard question: if humans are so wonderful, who captured Ruby and brought her here?
paragraphs.simple: Bob still does not believe Ruby’s story. He points out a problem: Ruby is here, in a cage at the mall. If humans are so nice, then who caught her, put her in a box, and sent her to this place?

paragraphs.context: Bad humans killed my family, and bad humans sent me here.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ruby says some humans are bad and some are good. Bad humans killed her family and sent her to the mall, but the humans who pulled her from the hole saved her.
paragraphs.simple: Ruby speaks in a strong voice. She says bad humans killed her family, and bad humans sent her here to the mall. But on the day she fell into the hole, it was humans who saved her. Those humans, she says, were good.

paragraphs.context: not going to let her die on him, not after all the money
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mack says the vet will come in the morning. He will not let Stella die — not after all the money he has spent on her.
paragraphs.simple: George tells Julia what Mack said on the phone. The animal doctor will come in the morning if Stella is not better. Mack says he will not let her die on him. He has put a lot of money into her, and he does not want to lose it.

paragraphs.context: promises are forever, and forever is an unusually long time.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stella has never asked anyone for a promise, because a promise lasts forever — and forever feels extra long when you live in a cage.
paragraphs.simple: Stella asks Ivan for a promise. She says she has never asked for a promise before. Promises are forever, and forever is a very, very long time. It feels even longer when you are living in a cage.

paragraphs.context: It would be easier to promise to stop eating, to stop breathing,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan feels this promise is almost impossible to keep. It would be easier to promise things no one can do.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan understands what Stella is asking: to take care of Ruby and give her a different life, somewhere safe, not here. He feels this is almost impossible. It would be easier to promise to stop eating, to stop breathing, or to stop being a gorilla.

paragraphs.context: I know it the way you know that summer is over
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan just knows Stella is dead, the way you just know winter is coming — a deep, sure feeling with no proof.
paragraphs.simple: Before Mack, before Bob, even before Ruby, Ivan knows Stella is gone. He knows it the way you know summer is over and winter is on its way. He cannot explain how he knows. He just knows.

paragraphs.context: I would give all the yogurt raisins in all the world
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan wishes he could stop feeling sad. He would give up everything for a cold heart that feels nothing.
paragraphs.simple: Stella once teased Ivan that gorilla hearts are made of ice and elephant hearts are made of fire — elephants feel more joy and more grief. Right now Ivan is full of grief. He says he would give all the yogurt raisins in all the world for a heart made of ice, a heart that cannot feel pain.

paragraphs.context: That Stella had a good and happy life? That she lived
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan cannot find honest words to comfort Ruby. He cannot truly say Stella had a happy life, or lived as she should have.
paragraphs.simple: All day Ivan tries to think of words to comfort Ruby. What can he say? That Stella had a good and happy life? That she lived the way she was meant to live? That she died with the ones who loved her nearby? He knows only the last one is true.

paragraphs.context: I can only hear a few of his words. Vet. Should have. Wrong.
paragraphs.mainIdea: George is angry at Mack. Ivan only hears broken words about the vet — “should have” and “wrong.”
paragraphs.simple: Julia cries all evening. When George sees Mack, he runs to him. Ivan cannot hear everything George says. He only hears a few broken words: vet, should have, wrong. George’s cheeks are wet, and he will not meet Ivan’s eyes.

paragraphs.context: We wait to see hints of what might yet be.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gorillas do not name a baby right away. They watch the baby first, waiting for signs of what the baby will be like.
paragraphs.simple: Gorillas do not give their newborn babies names right away, the way humans do. They get to know their babies first. They wait and watch for hints — small signs — of what the baby might become.

paragraphs.context: It held her like a vine, stretching across the miles, comforting, strangling.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan knew he had to let his old life die to keep living. His sister could not let go of home — it held her like a vine, both comforting and strangling her.
paragraphs.simple: After the humans captured Ivan and his sister, they were put in a dark crate. Ivan somehow knew that to live, he had to let his old life die. But his sister could not let go of their home. Home held her like a vine stretching across the miles. The vine was comforting, but it was also strangling her.

paragraphs.context: she looked at me without seeing, and I knew that
paragraphs.mainIdea: His sister died in the crate. She looked at Ivan without really seeing him, and he knew her tie to home had broken.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan and his sister were still in the crate when she looked at him without seeing — her eyes were open, but she was gone. Ivan knew then that the vine had finally snapped. Her hold on home had broken, and she had died.

paragraphs.context: I felt hungry for the skilled touch of a grooming friend,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan was not hungry for food. He ached for gorilla company — a friend’s grooming touch, play fights, the safety of his troop.
paragraphs.simple: In his new life with Mack and Helen, Ivan was well fed. But hunger comes in many shapes and colors — not just hunger for food. At night, alone in his pajamas, Ivan felt hungry for the touch of a grooming friend, for the happy grunts of a play fight, for the easy safety of his troop moving through the shadows together.

paragraphs.context: We need this job. Your mom, the doctor bills…
paragraphs.mainIdea: George cannot risk his job to help Ruby. His family needs the money to pay his wife’s doctor bills.
paragraphs.simple: Julia asks if they could call someone for help. George says he wishes he could help Ruby, but he would not know who to call. He needs this job, and Julia’s mother needs it too — there are doctor bills to pay. So George and Julia go back to work.

paragraphs.context: the half-formed words die in my throat.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan wants to lie to comfort Ruby, but the words will not come out. Instead he says she will not die here if he can stop it.
paragraphs.simple: Ruby asks Ivan if she will die in her domain someday, like Stella did. Once again Ivan thinks about lying, but when he looks at Ruby, the half-formed words die in his throat — he cannot say them. Instead he says: not if I can help it. Not if he can stop it.

paragraphs.context: I pause, and then I say it. “It’s a cage.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan finally says the true word. His home is not a “domain.” It is a cage.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan feels something tighten in his chest, something dark and hot. He has always called his home a domain. Now he pauses, and then he says it out loud: it is not a domain. It is a cage.

paragraphs.context: Then they chopped off their hands, their feet, their heads.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The humans cut off his mother and father’s hands, feet, and heads.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan remembers what the humans did. He and his sister were clinging to their mother when the humans killed her. Then they shot his father. Then they chopped off their hands, their feet, and their heads — the hands, feet, and heads of his mother and father.

paragraphs.context: I look at my fingers, coated in red paint
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan looks at his fingers, covered in red paint, and suddenly knows how to keep his promise.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan looks down at his fingers. They are covered in red paint, as red as blood. In that moment he understands what he must do to keep the promise he made.

paragraphs.context: He carries the claw-stick with him all the time now.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mack now carries the claw-stick everywhere, but he never uses it — Ruby is too frightened to disobey, so he doesn't need to.
paragraphs.simple: Mack takes the claw-stick with him wherever he goes now. He does not hit Ruby with it. He does not have to. Ruby no longer fights back, and she does everything Mack tells her to do.

paragraphs.context: I hide the paintings under my pool of dirty water
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan hides his paintings under his pool of dirty water so Mack will not find them and sell them in the gift shop.
paragraphs.simple: Before Mack can see the paintings, Ivan hides them under the dirty water in his pool. He does not want Mack to sell them in the gift shop for twenty dollars each, or twenty-five dollars with a frame. These paintings are for Ruby, every one of them.

paragraphs.context: He says he’s cutting back on our food.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mack says Ruby is not bringing in enough visitors, so he will give the animals less food and turn off their heat at night.
paragraphs.simple: More visitors are coming, but Mack says it is still not enough. He says Ruby is not doing her share of the work. To save money, he will give them less food, and he will turn off the heat in their cages at night.

paragraphs.context: It’s a wild cage. A zoo. I see where it begins,
paragraphs.mainIdea: On TV Ivan sees a zoo: a 'wild cage' with walls that keep the animals on one side and the people on the other.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan is watching an ad on TV. He sees a strange thing: a cage that is also wild. It is a zoo. He can see where the place starts and where it ends. A wall runs through it. The wall says: the animals stay here, the people stay there, and it will always be that way.

paragraphs.context: All those endless letters, those sticks and circles and zigzags,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Watching Julia do homework, Ivan thinks about human letters — endless sticks, circles, and zigzags everywhere — and gets an idea.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan watches Julia do her homework. He thinks about how gorillas live fine without spelling. Human writing is everywhere: books, magazines, billboards, candy wrappers. All those letters look like sticks and circles and zigzags to him. Then he jumps up. He has thought of something: a word.

paragraphs.context: Then I make two fat lines, like broom handles.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan paints two thick lines joined by a third line — the letter H, the first letter of the word HOME.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan studies the billboard, then starts to paint. He makes two thick lines that look like broom handles. Then he paints one more thick line to join them together. It is not a ladder. It is a letter: H. He needs to make three more letters.

paragraphs.context: I can’t let Ruby be another One and Only.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan realizes Ruby will stay in the mall forever, just like Stella did, and he refuses to let that happen.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan looks at Ruby sleeping. Suddenly he understands: she will never leave the Big Top Mall. She will stay here forever, just the way Stella stayed here all her life. Ivan decides he cannot let Ruby become another 'One and Only' — another animal who lives and dies alone in a cage.

paragraphs.context: A real chest beating sends the whole jungle running,
paragraphs.mainIdea: A real gorilla chest-beat is so loud and frightening that every animal in the jungle runs away.
paragraphs.simple: When visitors beat their chests, it is quiet and silly. But when a truly angry gorilla beats its chest, the sound is terrible. You would not want to hear it, even with earplugs in, even from three miles away. The noise sends every animal in the jungle running, as if the sky were breaking open or men with guns were coming.

paragraphs.context: “H, E, O. And that looks a lot like an eye.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Julia finds the letters H, E, O — and a painted eye, which she and George confuse with the letter I.
paragraphs.simple: Julia is putting the pictures in order. She finds the letter H, then E, then O. One picture looks a lot like an eye. George thinks it might be the letter I, and he even writes the letters in the air with his finger. But Julia says it is not a letter at all — it is a real eye, drawn in the painting. Next to it she sees something that looks like a foot, or a tree, or an elephant's trunk.

paragraphs.context: Maybe people will see the sign, and they’ll know
paragraphs.mainIdea: Julia hopes that people who see Ivan's billboard will understand Ruby does not belong in the mall and will want to help.
paragraphs.simple: Julia is not sure the sign will change anything. But maybe, she says, people will see it and understand that a baby elephant does not belong in a shopping mall. Maybe they will want to help Ruby too.

paragraphs.context: “Dad,” Julia says softly, “what if Ruby ends up like Stella?”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Julia's quiet question — what if Ruby dies here like Stella did — finally convinces George to help.
paragraphs.simple: Julia speaks softly to her father. She asks him: what will happen if Ruby stays here and ends up like Stella? George looks at Ivan, at Ruby, and at Julia. Then he drops the claw-stick. He agrees to help. The ladder is in the storage locker.

paragraphs.context: He trains his camera on the gleaming blade.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The cameraman notices the claw-stick and points his camera at its shiny blade.
paragraphs.simple: The cameraman walks through the mall filming everything. When he sees the claw-stick, he stops. He points his camera at the shiny blade and films it. Then he walks on.

paragraphs.context: “No, Ruby,” I say. “This is your prison.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ruby calls the mall her home, but Ivan tells her the painful truth: it is her prison.
paragraphs.simple: Ruby says she does not want to go to the zoo. She wants to stay with Ivan, Bob, and Julia. She says the mall is her home. Ivan answers: no, Ruby. This place is not your home. It is your prison.

paragraphs.context: His voice is bright, but his eyes are faraway and sad.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bob sounds cheerful, but his sad, distant eyes show he is hurting — he will miss Ivan.
paragraphs.simple: Bob talks in a bright, casual voice, as if nothing is wrong. But his eyes look far away and sad. He tells Ivan he will miss his stomach. Then he closes his eyes and makes a strange sound in his throat.

paragraphs.context: The last time I was in a box, my sister died.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan is afraid of the box because the last time he was put in one, his sister died.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan looks at the huge dark box. Now he understands how Ruby feels about her box. He does not want to go into this one. The last time he was in a box, his sister died.

paragraphs.context: “Mack fired my dad.” Tears slip down her cheeks.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Julia says goodbye: Mack fired George, but the zoo woman may find him cleaning work later.
paragraphs.simple: Julia runs to Ivan's cage at night. She presses her hand against the glass. She tells Ivan it is her last night. Mack fired her dad, and tears run down her face. But the zoo woman said there might be work for him at the zoo later — cleaning cages and things like that.

paragraphs.context: I’m not ready. I need more time.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan is shocked: he is leaving tomorrow and does not feel ready.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan is shocked by the news. He is leaving tomorrow. He feels he needs more time. He has not said good-bye to his friends. He has not thought it all through.

paragraphs.context: Mack pulls a small photo out of his shirt pocket.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mack shows Ivan an old photo of the two of them when Ivan was young.
paragraphs.simple: Mack takes a small picture from his shirt pocket. It shows Ivan as a young gorilla. Mack and Ivan sit together in the front seat of a car with a roof that can fold down.

paragraphs.context: Remember when we went on that roller coaster?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mack remembers the fun times he and Ivan shared long ago.
paragraphs.simple: Mack asks Ivan if he remembers their fun days together. They rode a roller coaster. Mack tried to teach Ivan to play basketball, but Ivan was very bad at shooting. Mack shakes his head and laughs as he remembers.

paragraphs.context: “I’m going to miss you, Ivan,” he says, and then he leaves.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mack says good-bye and walks away without looking back.
paragraphs.simple: Mack tells Ivan he will miss him. Then Mack leaves. He does not turn to look back at Ivan.

paragraphs.context: Some have white coats. Some have rustling papers.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Many humans arrive early in the morning, quiet and busy, ready to move the animals.
paragraphs.simple: Early in the morning, Maya comes with many other humans. Some wear white coats. Some carry papers that make a soft crackling sound. They are quiet, busy, and serious.

paragraphs.context: A part of me doesn’t want her to leave either
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan feels sad too, but he hides it so Ruby will feel brave.
paragraphs.simple: Part of Ivan does not want Ruby to go either. But he knows he must not tell her that. He wants to sound strong for her.

paragraphs.context: I hold her out to Bob. He tilts his head, confused.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan gives his old toy to Bob to comfort him.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan holds out Not-Tag to Bob. Bob tilts his head, confused. He does not understand why Ivan is giving him the toy.

paragraphs.context: The sun slices through the thick ceiling of trees
paragraphs.mainIdea: Drugged and sleepy, Ivan dreams of the jungle with his old family.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan falls asleep. He dreams he is with Tag. They swing from vines while Stella watches. In the dream, sunlight cuts through the leaves above like a ceiling. The wind tastes sweet like fruit.

paragraphs.context: I am in the grumbling belly of some great beast.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Half asleep, Ivan imagines the moving box is a giant animal's rumbling stomach.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan is half asleep. The box shakes and rumbles. In his sleepy mind, it feels as if he is inside the noisy belly of some huge animal.

paragraphs.context: It’s a new cage not unlike my old cage
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan wakes up in a new cage of glass and steel, much cleaner than his old one.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan wakes. He sees glass and steel around him. It is a new cage. It is much like his old cage, but much cleaner.

paragraphs.context: Is there anyone to tell her stories when she can’t get to sleep?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan worries that Ruby is lonely and has no one to comfort her.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan worries about Ruby. Is she in a cage like her old one? Is she alone, cold, hungry, sad? When she cannot sleep, is there anyone to tell her stories, the way Stella did?

paragraphs.context: I have no visitors here, no sticky-fingered children or weary parents.
paragraphs.mainIdea: At the zoo, no crowds come to stare at Ivan as they did at the mall.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan has no visitors here. At the mall, children with sticky hands and tired parents came to stare at him. Now nobody comes.

paragraphs.context: I taste it in the air, like faroff rain clouds gathering.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan senses that something is about to change.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan does not know what it is, but he feels a change coming. He senses it the way you can sense rain clouds gathering far away before a storm.

paragraphs.context: It’s a show about gorillas being gorillas.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Maya shows Ivan a film of real gorillas living naturally, without people.
paragraphs.simple: Maya turns on the TV. It is not a romance or a Western. It is a nature show with no human voices and no ads. It shows real gorillas eating, cleaning each other's fur, play-fighting, and sleeping. Ivan watches them do all these things.

paragraphs.context: without a silverback to protect them.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The gorilla family Ivan watches has no adult male leader to guard them.
paragraphs.simple: Every day Ivan watches the gorillas on the TV screen. It is a small, odd family: three females and one young male. There is no silverback, no grown male leader, to protect them.

paragraphs.context: They’re on the other side of the glass, watching me watching them.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The gorillas are real — behind the glass, looking back at Ivan as he looks at them.
paragraphs.simple: It is the same family Ivan watched on TV. But they are not on a screen. They are real, on the other side of the glass. They watch Ivan, and Ivan watches them.

paragraphs.context: Are they as fascinated by me as I am by them?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan wonders if the gorillas find him as interesting as he finds them.
paragraphs.simple: The gorillas stare at Ivan. They tilt their heads, point, and hoot. Ivan wonders: are they as amazed by me as I am amazed by them?

paragraphs.context: I admire her intact canines from afar.
paragraphs.mainIdea: From a safe distance, Ivan admires Kinyani's sharp, unbroken teeth.
paragraphs.simple: From far away, Ivan looks at Kinyani's long, sharp teeth. They are whole and unbroken, and he admires them.

paragraphs.context: I’m not ready to be a silverback.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan is afraid of becoming the family's leader.
paragraphs.simple: The humans lead Ivan to a door. Kinyani and the others wait on the other side. But Ivan feels he is not ready. He does not want to be a silverback, a leader. He just wants to be Ivan.

paragraphs.context: Ruby would want to know, and she would have been through that door by now.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan thinks Ruby would already have gone through the door.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan thinks of Ruby's endless curiosity. If Ruby were here, she would ask: what is on the other side of the door? Ruby would want to know. She would have walked through that door by now.

paragraphs.context: she’s testing me to see if I’m a true silverback
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kinyani is testing whether Ivan can be a strong leader who protects the family.
paragraphs.simple: Kinyani chases Ivan and throws a stick at him. Ivan understands: she is testing him. She wants to see if he is a true silverback, a strong leader who can protect her family.

paragraphs.context: I try to think past the babies and the motorbikes and the popcorn
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan tries to remember how real gorillas lived before his mall life.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan lies awake. He tries to remember what it was like to be a real gorilla. How did gorillas move? How did they touch? How did they know who was the boss? He tries to think past his mall life: the babies, the motorbikes, the popcorn, the short pants.

paragraphs.context: I grumble and swat and swagger.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan pretends to be a tough leader to impress the young male.
paragraphs.simple: The young male is eyeing Ivan's food hungrily. Ivan imagines being his father's son. He grumbles, swats, and walks proudly. He beats his chest till the whole world hears. Kinyani and the others watch.

paragraphs.context: grunting their disapproval: too small, too flimsy, an ugly thing to see.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The other gorillas grunt to show they think Ivan's nest is bad.
paragraphs.simple: The other gorillas watch Ivan build his nest. They grunt their disapproval. They think the nest is too small, too weak and thin, an ugly thing to see.

paragraphs.context: I see something new in Ruby’s eyes, and I know what it is.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan sees a new look in Ruby's eyes as she stands close to the other elephant.
paragraphs.simple: They stand side by side, just the way Stella and Ruby used to do. Their trunks are twisted together. Ivan sees something new in Ruby's eyes, and he knows what it is.

paragraphs.context: And then I realize what’s happening.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan suddenly understands that Kinyani is playing a game with him.
paragraphs.simple: Kinyani walks toward Ivan, taps his shoulder, and runs away on her knuckles. She comes back, pushes him, and dashes past. Then Ivan understands what is happening: they are playing. They are playing tag, and Ivan is it.

paragraphs.context: Her shoulder brushes mine, and we let the sun soak into our fur.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kinyani sits close to Ivan, showing that he is accepted into the family.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan finishes telling his troop his life story. They look away, silent. Then Kinyani moves closer. Her shoulder touches his. Together, they let the warm sun sink deep into their fur.

paragraphs.context: This is, after all, still a cage.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Even though the zoo is beautiful, Ivan knows it is still a cage.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan looks at the wall. It is high and wide, carefully built to keep the gorillas in and others out. It is clean and white and endless. Ivan thinks: after all, this is still a cage.

paragraphs.context: And the wall waits, like an endless blank billboard.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The big white wall looks like a blank sign waiting to be painted.
paragraphs.simple: The pile of dirt is soft to the touch. Ivan looks at the wall. It is white, clean, and endless. It waits like a huge blank signboard, ready for a picture.

paragraphs.context: I make swoops and swirls and thick lines.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan paints freely with mud, not caring what the picture becomes.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan slaps mud on the warm wall. He makes handprints and a noseprint. He slides his palms up and down. The mud is thick and hard to use, but he keeps going. He makes curving strokes, circles, and thick lines: shapes, light, and shadow. He does not know what he is making, and he does not care.

paragraphs.context: Not much color, but lots of movement.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan likes his mud painting: it feels wild and dreamlike.
paragraphs.simple: Ivan steps back to look at his work. He climbs a tree to see it better. The wall is splashed with mud. It has little color but much movement. Ivan likes it. It feels dreamy and wild, like a picture Julia might have made.

paragraphs.context: “She’s here, Stella,” I whisper. “Ruby’s safe.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ivan tells Stella that he kept his promise: Ruby is safe.
paragraphs.simple: From the hilltop, Ivan sees elephants far away. One is Ruby, standing belly-deep in tall grass with others by her side. Ivan whispers to Stella, who is gone: she is here. Ruby is safe, just as he promised.

paragraphs.context: She’s walking three extra dogs to cover my food.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bob explains how Julia manages to keep and feed him.
paragraphs.simple: Bob explains how he got here. George's zoo job does not start till next month. Until then, Julia walks three extra dogs to earn money. That money pays for Bob's food. And all three dogs are poodles.

paragraphs.context: She’s with other elephants now. Because of you.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Julia tells Ivan that Ruby is happy with other elephants, thanks to him.
paragraphs.simple: Julia holds up a little photo of Ruby. She tells Ivan: Ruby is with other elephants now. It is because of Ivan that Ruby has this new life.

paragraphs.context: She gestures toward me. “For this.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Julia thanks her father for Ivan's new life.
paragraphs.simple: Julia says good-bye to Ivan. She tells him to say hello to his new family. Then she turns to her father George and thanks him. When he asks what for, she points toward Ivan. She means: thank you for this, for Ivan's new home and family.

sentences.context: noble, contained, calm like a cobra is calm
sentences.grammar: The adjective "calm" is repeated ("calm like a cobra is calm") to stress that this quietness is the dangerous kind.
sentences.simple: The bull elephant was noble and quiet and controlled — but, like a cobra, his calm hid great danger.

sentences.context: Not that I hadn’t had visitors.
sentences.grammar: "Not that..." corrects what the reader might think after the last sentence; the next sentences explain the correction.
sentences.simple: Ivan does not mean that he never had visitors.

sentences.context: Sometimes I wish the glass were not there.
sentences.grammar: After "wish", "were" (not "was") marks an unreal wish: the glass is really there.
sentences.simple: Sometimes Ivan wishes there were no glass wall between him and the children.

sentences.context: who teases her too, but in a nice way
sentences.grammar: The sentence contrasts two kinds of teasing: Lila's mean teasing and Deshawn's friendly teasing.
sentences.simple: Deshawn also teases Julia, but his teasing is kind, not mean.

sentences.context: As if a silverback could ever be cute.
sentences.grammar: "As if" is sarcastic here: it dismisses the idea as ridiculous rather than making a real comparison.
sentences.simple: The idea that a silverback — huge and powerful — could be "cute" is silly.

sentences.context: Before Mack, before Bob, even before Ruby, I know
sentences.simple: I knew Stella was dead before Mack, Bob, or Ruby knew it.
sentences.grammar: Three “before” phrases are stacked at the front for emphasis; “is gone” is a gentle way of saying “is dead.”

sentences.context: She makes a noise that sends the sawdust scattering
sentences.simple: She makes such a loud, strong noise that the sawdust flies up all around her.
sentences.grammar: “Send” here means “cause to move”: the noise makes the sawdust scatter and fly.

sentences.context: Mack drops the claw-stick and falls down on the ground and curls
sentences.simple: Mack drops the stick, falls to the ground, curls up like a ball, and cries loudly like a baby.
sentences.grammar: A long chain of actions joined by “and”; the dashes hold Ivan’s guess about where Ruby hit Mack.

sentences.context: In the flicker of time it takes a snake’s tongue
sentences.simple: In less than a second — about as fast as a snake's tongue tasting the air — the hidden, angry Ivan could want revenge.
sentences.grammar: The pattern 'it takes X (time) to do Y' is packed into a noun phrase with 'that' left out: 'the flicker of time (that) it takes a snake's tongue to taste the air'.

sentences.context: soundless as the wet wings of a new butterfly
sentences.simple: They beat their chests without making any sound — as quiet as the wet wings of a butterfly that was just born.
sentences.grammar: Ellipsis in a comparison: 'soundless as X' means 'as soundless as X' — the first 'as' is left out.

sentences.context: Give him long enough and he’ll write a novel.
sentences.simple: If you give a chimp enough time, he will write a whole book.
sentences.grammar: An order + 'and' works as a condition: 'Give him long enough, and (= if you give him enough time) he'll write a novel.'

sentences.context: a sign that shows Ruby in a zoo with the word
sentences.simple: You want me to put up a big sign that shows Ruby in a zoo, with the giant word HOME written on it?
sentences.grammar: One long noun phrase with stacked modifiers: 'a sign' is described by 'that shows Ruby in a zoo', 'with the word home on it', and 'in giant letters' all at once.

sentences.context: a finger painting a two-year-old could do, I don’t know
sentences.simple: I don't understand why anyone would pay forty dollars for a finger painting that even a two-year-old could make.
sentences.grammar: Relative clause with 'that' left out: 'a finger painting (that) a two-year-old could do'.

sentences.context: even as I say these words, I remember with a shudder
sentences.simple: At the very moment I say this, I think with fear about the last box I was put in.
sentences.grammar: 'Even as' means 'at the same time as'; 'the last box I was in' leaves out 'that': 'the box (that) I was in'.

sentences.context: If I could use human words to say what I need
sentences.simple: If I were able to speak with human words, everything would be so easy.
sentences.grammar: Unreal conditional about the present: 'If I could (but I can't), this would (but it isn't)' — past verb forms describe something impossible now.

sentences.context: but never have they looked so happy
sentences.grammar: After 'never', 'have' comes before 'they' to make it stronger.
sentences.simple: but they have never looked this happy before.

sentences.context: she would have been through that door by now
sentences.grammar: 'Would have been' talks about something that surely would have happened earlier.
sentences.simple: She certainly would have walked through the door already.

sentences.context: I try to imagine Ivan as he might have been.
sentences.grammar: 'Might have been' imagines a different past: the Ivan that could have existed.
sentences.simple: I try to picture the Ivan I could have become.

sentences.context: I’m the silverback I’m pretending to be
sentences.grammar: The word 'that' is left out: 'the silverback (that) I'm pretending to be' tells more about 'silverback.'
sentences.simple: I am the silverback that I am only pretending to be.

sentences.context: Is there anything sweeter than the touch of another
sentences.grammar: This question wants no answer. It is a way of saying 'nothing is sweeter.'
sentences.simple: Nothing feels better than the touch of another gorilla.

sentences.context: like humans, prone to gossip and bad jokes
sentences.grammar: The part between the commas, 'prone to gossip and bad jokes,' tells more about 'humans.'
sentences.simple: Humans love to chatter, gossip, and tell bad jokes, but gorillas do not.

sentences.context: Near the top of the hill is a low-limbed tree
sentences.grammar: For a pretty description, the place comes first: 'Near the top of the hill' comes before 'is a tree with low branches.'
sentences.simple: A tree with low branches stands near the top of the hill.

sentences.context: in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo
sentences.grammar: 'What' here means 'the place that.' The whole part works like a naming word.
sentences.simple: in the place that is now called the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
